defaults.permitted_development: In Wales, small ancillary family accommodation may sometimes be achieved through ordinary extension rules or an incidental outbuilding, but a true self-contained annexe should not be assumed to be permitted development and will often need planning permission.

rules.height_rules: Where a detached ancillary building relies on outbuilding rights, the normal outbuilding height limits apply: up to 4m with more than one roof pitch, up to 3m with a single-pitch or other roof form, 2.5m for a flat roof, eaves up to 2.5m and 2.5m overall within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate annexe depth allowance. Attached accommodation must stay within the normal extension rules for the house, while detached space must stay within the curtilage and 50% coverage limits and still read as ancillary rather than a second home.
rules.boundary_rules: A detached incidental building should not sit forward of the principal elevation or a side elevation that comes closer to the highway than the house, or within 5m of it, whichever is nearer. Boundary siting also affects whether the building still looks ancillary or starts to read as a separate planning unit.
rules.roof_rules: A detached incidental building must remain single storey if it relies on outbuilding rights. Roof terraces, verandas, balconies and dominant house-like upper floors usually move the scheme outside the normal Welsh householder route.
rules.materials_rules: If permission is granted for annexe accommodation, expect conditions keeping it ancillary to the main dwelling. Materials, servicing, entrances and window layout should reinforce that relationship rather than suggest a freestanding new house.

restrictions.conservation_area: In Wales, conservation area controls and any Article 4 direction can remove normal householder permitted development rights for visible external work. Check the planning register before relying on national allowances.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be needed for internal or external works that affect the character of a listed building or its curtilage structures. Minor-looking changes can still need consent in Wales.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.permitted_development: The critical Welsh distinction is between ancillary accommodation tied to the main house and a separate planning unit. Once the space functions as self-contained living accommodation, a planning application is usually needed.

rules.height_rules: Detached ancillary space can only borrow the ordinary Welsh outbuilding height rules while it remains incidental: single storey, eaves no more than 2.5m, up to 4m with more than one roof pitch, up to 3m with another roof form and 2.5m overall near a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Instead of a dedicated annexe projection right, the Welsh route depends on form and use: extensions follow the normal house rules, while detached structures must stay within the usual outbuilding limits and remain clearly ancillary.
rules.boundary_rules: Where annexe-style space sits tight to a boundary, the authority will usually look at both scale and independence. Separate access, services and a self-contained layout point away from the ordinary householder route.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form matters because it can make the building look like a second dwelling. Single-storey, subordinate forms are the safest option in Wales; roof terraces and dominant upper-storey accommodation usually need a fuller planning route.
rules.materials_rules: The external treatment should show that the accommodation belongs to the same dwellinghouse plot. Separate-house cues such as autonomous servicing, an independent front-door arrangement and overtly domestic detailing can make the proposal harder to justify.

rules.permitted_development: Annexe proposals in Wales need to be treated cautiously. Householder rights may cover attached ancillary space or an incidental garden building, but they do not normally allow a separate self-contained residence within the plot.

rules.height_rules: If the proposal depends on Welsh outbuilding rights, keep to the standard single-storey envelope: eaves no higher than 2.5m, up to 4m overall for a roof with more than one pitch, up to 3m for other roof forms and 2.5m overall if any part sits within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is not the real annexe test in Wales. An attached scheme must satisfy the ordinary extension rules, while a detached building must remain within the curtilage and coverage limits and still be genuinely ancillary in use.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and highway siting matter for both bulk and independence of use. Detached buildings with their own facilities, access and close-boundary siting are harder to defend as ordinary incidental development.
rules.roof_rules: If the proposal depends on outbuilding rights, keep the roof low-key and subordinate. Terrace-style roofs, upper-storey accommodation and prominent house-like forms often indicate that a full planning application is the safer route.
rules.materials_rules: When permission is sought for annexe accommodation, authorities often keep the use tied to the main house. Design choices such as entrances, window pattern, materials and servicing should support that subordinate relationship.

rules.height_rules: Where a detached ancillary building relies on outbuilding rights, the normal outbuilding height limits apply: up to 4m with more than one roof pitch, up to 3m with a single-pitch or other roof form, 2.5m for a flat roof, eaves up to 2.5m and 2.5m overall within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate annexe depth allowance. Attached accommodation must stay within the normal extension rules for the house, while detached space must stay within the curtilage and 50% coverage limits and still read as ancillary rather than a second home.
rules.boundary_rules: A detached incidental building should not sit forward of the principal elevation or a side elevation that comes closer to the highway than the house, or within 5m of it, whichever is nearer. Boundary siting also affects whether the building still looks ancillary or starts to read as a separate planning unit.
rules.roof_rules: A detached incidental building must remain single storey if it relies on outbuilding rights. Roof terraces, verandas, balconies and dominant house-like upper floors usually move the scheme outside the normal Welsh householder route.
rules.materials_rules: If permission is granted for annexe accommodation, expect conditions keeping it ancillary to the main dwelling. Materials, servicing, entrances and window layout should reinforce that relationship rather than suggest a freestanding new house.

restrictions.conservation_area: In Wales, conservation area controls and any Article 4 direction can remove normal householder permitted development rights for visible external work. Check the planning register before relying on national allowances.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be needed for internal or external works that affect the character of a listed building or its curtilage structures. Minor-looking changes can still need consent in Wales.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.permitted_development: The critical Welsh distinction is between ancillary accommodation tied to the main house and a separate planning unit. Once the space functions as self-contained living accommodation, a planning application is usually needed.

rules.height_rules: Detached ancillary space can only borrow the ordinary Welsh outbuilding height rules while it remains incidental: single storey, eaves no more than 2.5m, up to 4m with more than one roof pitch, up to 3m with another roof form and 2.5m overall near a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Instead of a dedicated annexe projection right, the Welsh route depends on form and use: extensions follow the normal house rules, while detached structures must stay within the usual outbuilding limits and remain clearly ancillary.
rules.boundary_rules: Where annexe-style space sits tight to a boundary, the authority will usually look at both scale and independence. Separate access, services and a self-contained layout point away from the ordinary householder route.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form matters because it can make the building look like a second dwelling. Single-storey, subordinate forms are the safest option in Wales; roof terraces and dominant upper-storey accommodation usually need a fuller planning route.
rules.materials_rules: The external treatment should show that the accommodation belongs to the same dwellinghouse plot. Separate-house cues such as autonomous servicing, an independent front-door arrangement and overtly domestic detailing can make the proposal harder to justify.

rules.permitted_development: Annexe proposals in Wales need to be treated cautiously. Householder rights may cover attached ancillary space or an incidental garden building, but they do not normally allow a separate self-contained residence within the plot.

rules.height_rules: If the proposal depends on Welsh outbuilding rights, keep to the standard single-storey envelope: eaves no higher than 2.5m, up to 4m overall for a roof with more than one pitch, up to 3m for other roof forms and 2.5m overall if any part sits within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is not the real annexe test in Wales. An attached scheme must satisfy the ordinary extension rules, while a detached building must remain within the curtilage and coverage limits and still be genuinely ancillary in use.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and highway siting matter for both bulk and independence of use. Detached buildings with their own facilities, access and close-boundary siting are harder to defend as ordinary incidental development.
rules.roof_rules: If the proposal depends on outbuilding rights, keep the roof low-key and subordinate. Terrace-style roofs, upper-storey accommodation and prominent house-like forms often indicate that a full planning application is the safer route.
rules.materials_rules: When permission is sought for annexe accommodation, authorities often keep the use tied to the main house. Design choices such as entrances, window pattern, materials and servicing should support that subordinate relationship.
